title: Graphs: state, nodes, edges & reducers
summary: An agent is a loop: think, act, look at the result, decide again. A straight chain can't loop, so agents run on **graphs**: a shared **state**, **nodes** that read it and return partial updates, **edges** that decide what runs next, and **reducers** that say how updates merge. This module builds that foundation and turns the Nimbus support pipeline into a graph whose order lookup runs beside triage.
learn: **Why LangGraph**: a chain runs once; a graph can check its output and loop back
**State schemas**: TypedDict, Pydantic, dataclass and MessagesState, and partial updates
**Nodes**: functions, config and runtime context, Runnables as nodes, async nodes, names
**Edges**: sequences, fan-out in parallel, and wiring checked by compile()
**Reducers**: replace, operator.add, add_messages, custom reducers and Overwrite
**Running graphs**: invoke, stream modes, batch, diagrams
flow:
START ─┬─ triage ─────────┬─ draft_reply → END
       └─ look_up_order ──┘
state = {ticket, triage, order, order_note, reply, steps (operator.add)}   each node returns only the keys it changes

labs.explain:
Five taglines with a 3-word limit. A **chain** gets one pass and can't notice when the tagline is too long; a **graph** writes, checks and loops back with feedback, at most three times.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: An edge back to an earlier node: the loop.

Every way to write a **node**: a plain function (or one that returns nothing), one that reads `config` and the runtime **context**, any **Runnable**, and an **async** node, plus how nodes are named.

Two slow nodes **in a line** and **fanned out** (timed), and the wiring mistakes **compile()** catches.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

A Nimbus order runs through four nodes; two of them run **in the same step** and both write `notes`. The identical graph with four state schemas: no reducers, `operator.add` on notes only, on both lists, and a custom `edit_order` reducer that understands removals. One crashes, two silently produce the wrong order, one is right.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

path.title: Production path: Nimbus support graph v1
path.summary: The support pipeline from the LangChain track (triage → reply) becomes an explicit graph. The order lookup needs only the ticket text, so it starts at the same time as triage; the reply waits for both and now knows the order's real status. Every node returns a partial update and adds a line to `steps`, so each run can be streamed and checked node by node.

steps.title: State
steps.explain: `SupportState`: the ticket, the triage decision, the order record and a note about it, the reply, and `steps` (a list with `operator.add`: every node appends what it did).

notes.text: Each node adds a line; nothing is overwritten.

production: Keep state small and serialisable: from Module 5 it is checkpointed after every step.

steps.title: Nodes
steps.explain: `triage` reuses the pipeline's triage step (structured output with a retry); `look_up_order` finds an order id in the ticket and reads the order (no model); `draft_reply` sends safety tickets the approved fixed message and otherwise drafts a reply with the order facts attached.

notes.text: No model call: plain code, instant.

notes.match: ticket = state["ticket"] + (f"\n\n[Facts for the reply: {state['order_note']}]" if state.get("order_note") else "")
notes.text: The reply sees the real order.

production: Nodes that call models stay thin wrappers around chains that are tested on their own (the LangChain track's triage scorecard still applies).

steps.title: Edges
steps.explain: Two edges from START run `triage` and `look_up_order` in the same step; `add_edge(["triage", "look_up_order"], "draft_reply")` makes the reply wait for both.

notes.text: The join: waits for every incoming edge.

production: Draw the graph in the docs (Mermaid) so reviewers can see the flow without reading code.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.explain:
Same model and prompts on the 20 labelled tickets.

| | category right | reply states the real order status | calls / ticket | p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LCEL pipeline | 0.90 | 0/6 | 1.85 | 4.4 s |
| **support graph** | 0.95 | **3/6** | 1.85 | 5.2 s |

The category difference is run-to-run variation (same triage prompt). The graph's replies can state the real order status because the lookup ran beside triage; half of them did. Having the facts isn't using them: Module 2 adds a check that sends such drafts back.
production: Measure the node you changed, not just the end result: here triage didn't change, the reply did.
